samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Edwin Leferink was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: I was living in Cleveland. And I was working for the Erie Railroad Company as a clerk in the treasurer's office. And --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How old were you then?

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: I guess about 17 or 18. I've -- yeah, I hadn't turned 21 yet, I don't think. You know, I was just a kid.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you were out of school at that point?

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: Oh, I was out of school, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you graduate early, or did you drop out?

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: No, no, I worked at Parker Appliance. I took a course at Collinwood for machine shop and that, and Tony Adamle was the crib attendant. And he used to play professional football for the Browns, and I took and learned how to run a screw machine and drill presses and that and different tools. And I got a job with Parker Appliance my last year of school.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: And I worked nights and went to school, and I graduated from John Adams in '41.

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: Yeah, yeah, uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you have specific memories of December 7, 1941?

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: Well, we were at a -- that Sunday, we were at a party. It was -- I don't know, it was after, you know, a preparty, we were out on a lake with some friend's house. And we stayed out Saturday night. And then Sunday morning, we got up and everything, had the radio on, and we heard oh, boy, then the fun started. But it was interesting. It was different. You know, I still think they were antagonized to start the war. I'm not -- we treated them pretty good. We took their metal away from them and did a lot of nasty things. And I think we had to -- eventually, we were going to get into the war regardless of what you say because we had to help England. And the Japanese was just an added problem, you know, so --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you had been following the news closely enough that you knew it was inevitable that we would --

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: Oh, yeah, eventually, you knew darn well you were going to get into this mess. Roosevelt didn't want to. But then again, I think you read history, Churchill, he was -- he was right on Roosevelt's butt, you know, hey, you have to -- and they didn't come right out with it, you know, Lend-Lease, jeez, we give them 50 destroyers, and we were shipping stuff to them, you know, I'd be ticked off if I was the Germans too, you know. And then the Japs, what they did to them, it just -- history, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When you heard it was Pearl Harbor, did you know where Pearl Harbor was?

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: Yeah, I had an idea. Well, I knew it was out in the Pacific. I didn't know the exact location, you know, but we knew it was in the vicinity of Hawaii because we had -- there was a kid on the street where we lived was in the Navy. And he was out there, but he didn't -- you know, he didn't get hurt. He wasn't in the area, but he was on a -- I don't know what, carrier or something. But my neighbor right down the street here, he was there, Tony Bompain, (ph) and it was pretty devastating. He -- I talk to him once in a while, but he don't like to talk about it. But he does have a license plate says Pearl Harbor survivor, you know. But he is a little older than I am.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was your personal reaction when you heard the news?

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: Well, I figured well, they're going to get me, you know. I didn't go down and enlist. I went down and checked, but I didn't go in and actually per se, I didn't actually enlist. And then -- finally I signed up, I was in the draft. I signed up, that's what happened, they took me into the draft in February 13, 1943.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you have job deferments because of your railroad --

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: No, no, no, I wasn't an engineer, I worked in the office. We were expendable. They could always get girls in, which they did. They hired a lot of women, and when we -- but when I come back, why, I didn't go in a job I had when I left, but I, you know, I was promoted and I -- the company treated us pretty good. We got -- you know, we got jobs, and we -- more money, but anything was better than what the Army was paying us. But that was a shock, $21 a month, you know. But that's the way the -- the way it went, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: In that year or so before you went in, before you were drafted, did you get involved in the war effort in any way on the home front?

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: No. No. I did my job, and we had the treasurer's office, we had -- I worked on like cash and that and helped. I was office boy. Then I got a clerking job. And we had a lot of bills coming in where the government was paying us, you know, transportation, hauling troops and that. And you had to -- we'd get checks, then you had to match them. I had that job for a little while, just, you know, my normal every day rationing and stuff like that. And I was an only child, I had my mother and dad, you know. It was hard when I went. They were very upset. And they were older, you know, and my dad worked for the railroad. And he worked -- he was a track -- out on the track section. He was a welder and did stuff like that. But --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Rationing wasn't much of a hardship for you?

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: Not at the time. Not at the time. I mean, well, gasoline, I was young, I wanted to use the car, you know. But you had buses and things like that, you know. But we were busy. I kept busy, I was working. And like I say, I was working at Parker Appliance. Then I got on with the Erie, and from there, you know, just went on. Then I went in the Service, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: All right. So you were drafted in February of '43?

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: Yes, 13th, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Tell me about that, tell me about your training?

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: Oh, it was cold. I can remember it was a cold February night. We caught the train at a terminal tower in Cleveland. My mother and dad were there. And we had our little overnight bag, you know, you had your extra pair of shorts and stuff and shaving stuff, and dressed up, it was winter. And we got out to Camp Huron, darn near froze to death, you know. I thought I had warm clothes, but when we got out there and that wind coming off the lake. Then when we switched from them civilian clothes into the Army, and it was a big difference because everything was wool. And you just get used to it, but they didn't take long to tell you you weren't a civilian any more. Boy, they got right on you. The shots and that, and then all kinds of tests we had to take. And I was lucky, out of the group that I went out with, I think I was the only one that got the Air Force. The rest of them went other places which was fortunate. But I think maybe my mechanical training that I had and stuff like that, I knew how -- I knew how to use tools. My dad was -- used tools and that, and I knew how to use a hammer and a screwdriver, knew what they were for. So maybe that was what got me into the Air Force. And I wasn't big, big tall guy like a lot of the guys, you know. But I can remember our shots, a great big clown was kidding, oh, wait until you get that shot. When he got shot, he passed out, but I didn't. And everyone laughed at him. Paybacks, you know. And then from there, we went to Florida.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was the Army Air Force your preference?

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: No, I really didn't have any preference, you know, hey, I was a draftee. I went -- was going to go where I was sent. The guys that enlisted, they could pick the Marines, the Navy, the Army, whatever, Air Force, whatever they want. But I was a draftee, you went where they told you, and I think I got the luck of the roll. I went -- qualified, and I got sent to Florida, and ended up in Air Corps training down there, basic, which three or four weeks, run around diving into the sand and stuff, you know, playing with wooden rifles. They had the big cumbersome things you run with, and we had no real rifles. And we took more tests and stuff, and I was sent to Chanute Field after my basic. And I took a basic mechanical thing with tools, a sheet metal course and stuff like that. And that was interesting. I did a lot, you know, I was -- learned different things, and still you were -- was hammered you in the Army, you had rules, and we did get to Chanute, they did let us go out. We got to Chicago a couple times. Chanute's located by Rand Tool, the University of Illinois is there. And but we went up to Chicago, they had a USO that you couldn't buy a drink, you couldn't do nothing. If you had a uniform on in Chicago, you'd go into a bar, go into a restaurant, you know, oh, the check is taken care of and stuff. It was real nice. Then they used to bring the girls, and I remember Glenn Miller was -- the Army band was there. And they had a dance, they brought all these college girls, cleaned out a hangar, moved everything out. And they had this big -- brought them in with busloads, had their mothers with them, chaperones, and it was just a good time. And the music, you know, music of our time. But it was interesting.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was your favorite Glenn Miller song?

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: Moonlight Serenade, Sunrise Serenade, you know, I liked all of them. Miller's music was good. There was all good bands at that time. We don't have them good bands nowadays, outside of Channel 91.5 up in Bainbridge. I don't know if you listen to them or not, they play that old music, and it brings back a lot of the favorites, you know, they talk about.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: As far as being thrown into basic training with guys from all over the country, was that much of an adjustment?

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: Well, no, not really, I mean, I never had any trouble with it. I don't know -- I know a lot of guys were homesick. Oh, crying. Going on that train down to Florida, we had one guy, guy that kept everyone up all night, someone give him a hot foot. We never saw him after that, he got his foot burned pretty good. You had them big GI shoes on and that gets pretty warm. We never did see the guy after that. But guys were homesick. And they weren't used to eating, you know, the Army food. It was different. They wanted to get the excess weight off of you. And they wanted to get you a lot of PT, physical ed., they'd get you out there and doing jumping jacks and pushups and marching. You never walked, you always run, run, run, you know. And you ate your chow at certain times, you didn't snack in between, you know. But it was different.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: The guy getting the hot foot, they did that because he was crying and they were teasing him?

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: Well, he finally went to sleep and someone was, well, I'll fix you, and they snuck over. More, you know, we were sleeping half of us, we didn't get any sleep, this guy talked and yacked and oh, look at this, look at that. Well, you know --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: He wasn't upset, he was just talking?

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: Yeah, he was just driving everyone nuts, you know. Some guy figured, you bugger, you kept me up all night, you're not going to sleep. And they gave him a hot foot. It was quite -- they made a stink about it. I felt sorry for the guy, but you try taking one of them boots off when it's kind of warm, you know, high tops. I never used to -- never wore something like that, them high top boots. But --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: The guys doing it get in trouble?

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: No one knew who did it. You're not going to -- no one is going to say who did it, but someone got him. But I can remember, he was about in the middle of the car, and boy, there was an awful commotion, this guy's hollering and screaming, he jumped around. Then we got to Florida, he couldn't hardly walk, his foot was pretty well swollen up and, you know, blistered. They took him off the train, and that's the last we ever saw him. No one ever found out who had did it. But we lived in a motel, big hotel, right by the pier in St. Petersburg. And from there, they took us out to -- what the heck was that. Some golf course, we lived in tents. And that was different, you know. You know, I never camped when I was a kid, you know, my folks were old, we never did that. But once I got married, had kids of my own, we camped a lot, but that was a -- different. When it rains, you got wet. When the wind blew, you got -- but it was different. Everything -- they broke your -- they got rid of you as a civilian. They made you -- actually, they made a lot of guys men, you know, they -- some of them were momma's boys. And my folks, I got along good with my folks. They depended on me a lot because of their age. And I was a little more mature, I guess, than some of the guys. Some of them were, you know, kids, never been away from home before. And that does get to you. But once I finished Chanute, why, then we ended up going up to Detroit, and I went to U.S. rubber school. It was teaching us about gas bags, the gas tanks for airplanes. We had to learn how to repair them and how to install them. It was a couple weeks maybe we were there. And from there, I went to Rapid City, South Dakota, and was assigned to an Army Air Base, and we had B-17s there. And I was assigned to a line crew, and you learned -- you were taught. You had guys there that knew these airplanes, and you learned a lot. Them were radial engines, great big Wright Cyclone engines. I can remember, you look at that thing, holy Nellie, it had four of them suckers on, you know, two on each side of the wing. And I was there a while, and then this group was alerted to go overseas. That's part of the training I guess. And we were getting our training, we were going to -- the whole gang of us I guess were going to go to Europe, but it never happened. They come in the barracks in the middle of the night and hustled -- anyone was an AM mechanic because they took us to Camp Stoneman -- or Camp Kearns, out in Salt Lake, Utah, and they give us overseas training. And that's the first time I got to fire a piece while I was in the Service, and I was trained on a -- it was carbine, and you had to tear it apart and put it back together again. And that was one day's training, and then the next day, we had to fire on the range and qualify. And in the meantime, they marched us up and down them stupid mountains and running and that. And then we were there oh, maybe a month. And from there, we went to Stoneman, Camp Stoneman in Frisco. And all kinds of tests and more shots, and then they put us on a boat, and it was the USS Monterey. It was a big cruise ship. And they stripped it pretty good, you know. They turned it into an Army troop ship, and everything was stand in line. You stood up when you ate. And seasick, guys were sick, oh, boy. We were tied up at the pier, and it was really something. The boat would go up, you'd look at the roof of the big long pier, the wharf there. And then it would go down, and you'd look at the pilings under. And guys were standing on the rail, and they'd get green and they'd start throwing up. But I never got seasick. I was --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's just when you were still tied up?

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: Yeah, we were still tied up at a stupid pier, you know. And then we took off, there was -- I can remember there was three huge cruise ships. And we went under the Golden Gate Bridge, and we got out into the ocean, and they all disappeared. And we never saw another ship until we pulled up in New Guinea. Milne Bay, New Guinea, and here comes -- and the three of us were back together again. And we had no escort on the way over. And they had blackouts, no smoking on the deck. And they had crews that went around, were assigned, they were the armed guard. You went around, make sure all the port holes were closed and guys weren't being stupid up on the top, lighting cigarettes, you know. And they had -- we had everything, we had nurses on board, pilots, and but they were all Army personnel. They didn't have any -- there was no Marines, it was just strict -- this boat I was on was all Army. We went to Milne Bay in Nadzab, and I ended up in a fighter squadron.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were there any sub scares or any problems in the crossing?

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: Oh, they had -- a couple times, they weren't alerts, general quarters. I didn't see any guns on that boat. They relied on speed. They were like I guess -- well, a buddy of mine went over on the Queen Elizabeth, and he said boy, that thing you could hear them thumping all night, they moved. This boat did the same thing. They didn't fool around. But they had no armed escort on. They had sailors on there that were -- I think they had maybe a gun in the back end, I don't know what good it would have done, you know, a big boat like that, but we were lucky, we got over there and unloaded. And that was the last we ever saw of that boat again. It was gone. But --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you were assigned to a fighter squadron, which squadron was that?

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: It was the Eighth Fighter Group, 35th Fighter Squadron in the Fifth Air Force, and they were -- they were an old all regular Army, these guys were that were in there. And enlisted men, they had a few guys that enlisted and joined, and then they started to get draftees like myself. And there was no -- no problems, you know. They accepted us. Hey, you know, they accepted you, you were an Army guy, you were an Air Force guy, and whether you enlisted or you're drafted, they didn't give a darn, just as long as you did your job, and it worked. We were assigned -- I was assigned to a line crew again. And I was given a tent. I met -- a guy in my tent was Coffin, Ed Coffin from Garfield Heights, Ohio, and him and I become buddies. And he -- I don't know where he is, he's living in Florida now. But we got separated. He got married, he went his way and we went our way, you know. And but him and I were together all the -- from the moment when I got overseas. He went home a month ahead of me. He had more time, he was there earlier than I was. But he was enlisted. He volunteered, and he went home a month ahead of me.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was it your preference to be on a ground crew, or did you try to get into a flight group?

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: Well, when we were in the bomber group, they had extensive schools for gunnery and that, but they wanted people -- the way I looked at it, they wanted people to know how to shoot. And I did get to fly a few times, fly like a training mission as a gunner. But like per se, I never became an actual aerial gunner. I mean them guys were good. Those guys had a lot of training, and they had to know, but we did -- they had stands out there where they would -- the regular gunners would practice and shoot, and then they would fly. But I did get to go up a couple times, you know, and fly, shoot them, you know. But I was happy where I was, you know, I was a mechanic. But it was a different, big -- you're working radial engines, and I got in fighters. The only one that had a radial engine as a fighters was the P-47. We didn't have too many of them in the Pacific, we had inline engines. And the first plane I worked on over there was a P-39. It was built up in Buffalo, I guess. Airacobra. Anyhow, it had a 37 mm cannon in the nose. And the engine was behind the pilot. He sat -- straddled the crankshaft. And that nose was filled with shells and guns, but it was not the Japs, they were not a good combat airplane. That's all we had, practically. They lost a lot of planes in Pearl Harbor, and then we got rid of them, and we got P-40s. Those are the ones that the Flying Tigers, you know, where people can really -- to what they were, and they were a good airplane, but they weren't any good at high altitude. They were -- our pilots loved them, they were good fighting planes. Our pilots did pretty good with them. And they -- then we got our big P-38s. Boy, that was like a difference between -- that's difference between driving an Austin and a Cadillac. Okay. That was two big main line -- two big engines and the booms, super chargers, they had 20 mm cannon on it, and they had four 50s in the nose, and that sucker could really -- it was -- it wasn't maneuverable like people say well, they see pictures of the P-51 and they see them flying, they're rolling. P-38 was a big airplane, and it needed room to maneuver. Our pilots were pretty good. They always flew in echelons of four, one was a shooter, one would protect them. And they just -- it was a beautiful ship, and it -- the pilots we had were good. They were all regular Army. And we started getting the 90 Day Wonders in later. That was '44, '45, but ours -- and as these guys got their time, they were rotated and they went home. But the enlisted men, they stayed, you know. You were there for more or less the duration. And then some of the guys, they got sick or something, they'd send them home.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When did you make that crossing to New Guinea, when did you arrive in New Guinea?

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: Oh, early part of '44.

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: Yeah, I spent I think it was 13 months and a few days in school in training here in the States, and then I spent 20 months --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Overseas?

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: -- overseas in combat zone with the Air Force with my fighter squadron.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That first base was where in New Guinea?

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: In Milne Bay, it was Nadzab. It was -- our outfit come out of -- they were there, they were up by Darwin, which is in northern Australia, and then they come over to New Guinea. And they were on one side of the Owen Stanley Mountains, and there was -- they call them one mile, two mile, three mile strips, the guys I was telling about, and when they'd have a red alert, the Japs would come in. The planes would take off to Darwin, and the guys would head for the hills. And they'd come in, they'd bomb the strip. They'd come back and repair the strip, then our planes would come back because, you know, they just didn't have the men and the material then, you know. You have to understand, everything was Europe, and I think that was one of the reasons they cleaned our group out and took all the mechanics and that because they were starting to go -- they had to go on the offensive and stop the Japs. The Marines had already stopped them in Guadalcanal, and then they had to consolidate. And then there was that big Coral Sea battle, that was a big fight. I don't know if we won it or lost, they claim we won it. But they stopped the Japs because they were -- I think they were pretty afraid, the more you read of history -- the Japs getting into Australia. And that would have been the end of -- and they stopped them, and then they started, they took -- the first parachute jump I think in the war was in New Guinea, they dropped -- they parachuted in and took Nadzab, and we come in on -- we flew -- our outfit always, we had advance air echelon, they had a rear echelon. The advanced echelon would go by boat most of the time and set up air cover because everything on the invasions was strictly Navy, and you know, they did the protecting because the -- they were a unit, they knew how to do this. And our planes would help protect the area, they'd go out strafe, and they had their assignments that they did. And these advanced echelons, they were a lot of fun, you travelled by boat, and you'd get up, you could watch a few of the invasion, we were sitting out in the bay while they were bombing and going in. And then we'd come in later in the day, and then you'd get on shore. You didn't know what you were going to get into or what you were going to do. Some guy helped unload boats, they wanted stuff to come out. Well, they just grab you and you were there, you know, hey, that's what you did. And then we'd get ready once the infantry took the strip or secured it, we'd get ready for our planes because, you know, didn't want them carriers around, they wanted to get them -- which was the smart way to do it. And they were limited. You know, they didn't have all the -- half the battleships were sitting in Pearl Harbor. And they were -- the biggest ship I saw there when I first went was a couple of cruisers. I didn't see any battleships, some cruisers and a lot of destroyers. And they did a wonderful job, you know, with what they had. And it took a while. And then them Liberty ships come along, they were -- they were a pain in the butt. You know, the only way you could get up them was up a Jacob's ladder. You had your pack on your back, then you go up and when you come off, you had to do the same thing. And the sea would go up, the boat would go up, the barge would go down, you'd be, you know, the infantry guys, I -- they had to do that. I felt sorry for some of them, you see them, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you go ashore landing craft, though?

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: Yeah, a couple of times, but most of the time, we rode -- we rode LSTs, they were landing ship tank, they had -- the bow would open up and we would drive our equipment, put it inside the tank deck. We'd have -- jeez, we'd have airplane -- aviation gas, barrels of it. Ammunition, bombs and stuff. Machine gun stuff, parts, all of our trucks. We'd have our tents and everything in there. They'd have them in the hole. Topside, they'd have boats and that. And them things just plugged along. They were not fast. And the best place on an LST was to sleep topside which we could do unless it was real bad. One time we ran in, they had -- we were -- I forget where we were, we ran into like hurricanes. And boy, them boats, the bow come out and the stern come out and you'd hear thump, thump, thump, and guys seasick, their heads in the John. If the boat didn't -- the bow didn't come up, they'd get their air. If the bow would come down, the head would be in the water. And but when it was a storm, real bad, you'd go down -- they'd make you go down into the quarters, but they were a relatively safe boat. They pull right up on the shore and drop their ramp, open the bow and drop their ramp, that was interesting. And then another ship we went on, was an AKE -- I can't remember all the number, but it was built on a cruiser's frame, and it had turrets on it, big five-inch guns on it, and they had two forward and one aft. And there the back end opened up, and there's two back doors open, and this big ramp dropped down. Well, a lot of places, like in the islands, they had this thing called a DUKW, and it would go on sea or land. And it had rubber wheels. It also had a propeller for water, propel it. They'd load that thing up with supplies, and they'd come right up to that ship and drive right up the ramp and unload, and then go back and get another load, you know, that's what they did. And then a lot of times, they'd have barges, they just come up to the ramp, and they'd drop their thing and you'd run up. That's how our personnel come on in barges, and we just went right up and walked up the ramp, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was your crew assigned to a particular airplane?

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: Yeah. Eventually, once you became a crew chief, you had a lot of training. It was, you know, it was a big responsibility. That guy's life was in your hands, and you had to know what you were doing. And our biggest problem, I can remember looking for parts. Boy, you'd see another airplane, you'd scavenge, go and steal anything that wasn't nailed down if you could use it. I know. Then we had a big fat cat, it was a great big -- it was a war weary bomber, and that bomber, they'd send for supplies. And we'd go down to different places and pick up supplies for our airplane, like parts and that what we needed. Then they'd send a pilot and an officer, enlisted man, we'd go down, load up that plane, and fly back. And they also used it for like when we were closer to Australia, some of the older guys were allowed to go and they had -- they could go for a week, and they'd fly them down in that. And they had a C-47, one of them old C-47s, and they -- a bunch of the guys from our group were going in that. And they disappeared, they don't know what happened to them, they never -- because the way they fought in the Pacific, they bypassed a lot of stuff. They didn't fight for every island, you know. They had certain targets, and that's what they went after and the rest, they isolated them like Rabaul. Later on, they went in, but they isolated that. I know our planes flew a lot of missions over Rabaul. Strafing and bombing and stuff like that. But that was the big -- eventually, you got your own plane. I got my own plane, I had a P-38 that I crewed. And it was interesting. But you had your -- you had some real important people, they called them -- they were a line chief. This guy is supposed to know everything. And they would come up, and they'd watch you, they'd check your plane, make sure, you know, you got problems. And if you had a problem, you had an engineering officer, you could always go to him, and it helped, you know, and you learned. An inline engine is different than a radial engine, you had to learn how -- what the different parts was. And you worked on them, and they taught you. And if you got in trouble, like we had our planes were flying out of this one island, they were going to Borneo, and that was approximately 1,200 miles round trip, that's a long time to sit in an airplane, you know. And they would get over, they'd find their group. Well, they never -- we had belly tanks they use to hang on, they had one with a 365 gallon, and the other I think was 125 gallon, and they'd hang them under the wings. And they also had bombs and everything else underneath them wings. And when they take off and land, they take off and land on their main tanks. And when they get airborne and they're lined up, then they go to the belly tanks, and you suck them dry. And then when they're -- then you go out to the wing tanks, and you would work your way back. And in case you got in combat, you dropped your belly tanks, get rid of them things, you know. And a lot of times, they come back with empty belly tanks, but a lot of times, they just drop them. Our planes were coming back and running out of fuel. And this Charles Lindbergh was working for Lockheed, he was -- a lot of people didn't like him because he was a -- they thought he was -- favored the Nazis, and he was on their list. But that guy was a pilot. He was 50 some years old I guess, he was no spring chicken, but he could fly airplanes. And he come in and taught these pilots fuel consumption, how to -- you can take and set the -- regulate the pitch control and you can cruise, use your different speeds. And he took our -- the one plane we crewed, and we flew it up just like he was going on a simulated mission. We topped the gas tanks off before they went, we drained them. Every morning when you went down, you drained all the gas tanks because condensation, you're bringing this gas out of barrels a lot of times, there's condensation in them. You have to make sure the water gets out of the gas, and you'd start on one wing tip, and you'd go down and open all the pet cocks. Then you go down the other end, by the time you get on the other end, open that up, this should be running pure gas. You go up, pour it, and then you'd shut it off and go back and shut everything off. Then you had a safety then, they have the nuts on the wings would have little holes, and you'd use copper wire and you'd twist it and then -- the vibration from flying in the airplane wouldn't let that open up. All your nuts and bolts on them airplanes were all -- that's the way they did, they safetied them. You went around, and it was quite an experience. He took this plane up, and he went up early in the morning, just like he was going on a mission. Did everything he had to do, come back, landed the plane. And then we went and drained the tanks. I think they got something like maybe 10, 12, 15 gallons of fuel that was left that he didn't run out of fuel. He showed it can be done. Then our squadron shut down for I think three or four days, and they went to school and they showed all these pilots and saved a lot of lives. He flew a couple missions with our guys.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: He flew combat missions?

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: Oh, yeah, you know, they say well, he didn't, but he did. I know he flew with our group. And he was quite a guy. He was friendly, you know, and you could ask questions, but that's what he was trained for, he knew airplanes and he could fly them.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you talk to him?

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: Oh, I talked to him a couple times, you know, but you know, just come down, and you help him. Your pilots, you're like a valet, valet to them, you help them get this chute on and that -- they're cumbersome. And you make sure his oxygen is hooked up, and the windshield is clean and that, and you always wish them, well, good luck, and then when he's up there, you know, you give him thumb's up, and then they'll taxi away down to the thing, and then you stand there and you watch your plane take off, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Where was this that you got close to Lindbergh?

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: That was in Morotai, when I was in the Isle of Morotai, they were flying from there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Is that in a particular chain that I would know?

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: I think that was -- I think that was Halmaheras. Where in the heck was -- let's see.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: If that's in the written account --

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: Biak. Biak. Biak was the first island we hit, that was in the (Shelton?) group. Then we went from there, we went to Morotai. Yeah, that was in the Halmaheras. We went in there, just an island, it was big coconut groves. It was owned by some coconut outfit that owned palm trees that grew coconuts.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: At the time Lindbergh was simply a consultant with an --

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: That's right, he was a consultant. Yeah, well --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: With Lockheed?

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: Yeah, with Lockheed, that's what he was, that was his big thing, and he did a lot. He did a lot of good, he went around to different squadrons, and they had problems, he went and talked to them and showed them what, you know, but I learned a lot.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did he get any confirmed kills?

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: I think he did, but they hush it up because, you know, he's a civilian, he could be in big trouble, you know, someone, you know, using civilians -- excuse me, that's against the Geneva Convention or some baloney, but he was a good pilot, and the pilots liked him. They looked up to him. I don't know if they -- what they thought, but I thought he was a pretty good man. He did what he was supposed to do.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you get close to any of your pilots?

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: Oh, yeah, you get close to them, you know, you're not buddy buddies. They have their group, and you had your group. But I never had any problem with pilots. They come down if they had a complaint, they would red line the plane, they would tell you this isn't working right and that. Okay. You'd write it up and then you'd check it. And we had one pilot, I can remember, every time he took that plane up, there was something wrong with it, you know. And when you run into that, you turn it over to the engineering officer, let him worry about it. And eventually, what happened is I was having trouble with a pilot because he said the struts weren't -- the old man took the plane up, and he flew it, almost flew the wheels off of it. There was nothing wrong with that plane, he put it back in service. That's all you can do, you know. But you never had any problem, you get in, you always wish them luck and they were a good bunch. Like I say, I was fortunate. We had pilots that were old, they were experienced, they were regular Army. And they had some that were -- they had some flying sergeants, and they commissioned them, you know, warrant officer and some of them became officers, you know. But it was different, you know. But you're not as close to them as you were to the guys you worked with every day, you know. Different things happen to us, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you lose any pilots?

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: Oh, yeah, we lost some pilots. We lost a few. And they were, you know, combat, you're going in, they're going in, you know, they're going in strafe and you're close, you know, they shoot back at you. And the Japs were good pilots. But they shot their wad, they ran out of experienced pilots, and that's where -- why they resorted more or less to the Kamikazes, those guys were crazy. You know, and then they had -- I only seen -- we saw a couple times, they had a -- I can't remember, I think it was a backup bomb, they call it. One guy --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: + bomb or something?

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: One guy sat -- one guy sat in the dumb thing, and they release him, and then he'd pick a target and dive at it. I seen where he made big holes in the ground, you know. But the Kamikazes, the one that hit us on our boat at Mindoro.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right. Tell me that, yes?

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: Well, we had went in at Morotai, and then they invaded the Philippines. And we ended up -- we loaded up, advanced echelon, went up to Tacloban, up in Leyte. END OF SESSION ONE, CD. BEGIN SESSION TWO, CD. LEFERINK: And oh, big fanfare, MacArthur was there, you know, all this baloney, we were on a strip. And that was our first real time that Kamikazes actually -- they were after the fleet because the fleet was there. But the weather was bad. And our planes were out fighter sweeping around, you know, trying to go after these air fields that were sweeping and bombing runs and that because they try to catch the Japs on the ground. And we were also helping the Navy, they were patrolling. Because if you flew over a Navy ship, regardless of who you were, you got shot at, with the Kamikazes, they didn't -- if it had wings and made noise, they shot at it, you know, which is hey, I would, too, you know, if I was sitting on a boat somewhere. But then the weather turned bad. One of our planes had to land at Tacloban, and the strip was like all mud. He got stuck, you know. He -- couldn't get him out. Well, then they decided I guess they went down. They went down, and they decided to take the island of Mindoro, that was a little thing, and we had good air cover, Japanese, 24 hours all the way. And they went into Mindoro. And we were sitting out in harbor, and I think it was the U.S. New Jersey was there, and they were shelling and bombing, and the infantry went in, and they secured the beachhead and that. And we were sitting there waiting to go in and unload because they had a small strip there. And they wanted that strip. And they did -- well, in the meantime, we were sitting there, we were on general quarters, but not the full general quarters, you know, the guys were on -- the Navy guys were on their guns. And I was assigned to this one crew to help with slide ammunition so the loader could help him. Anyhow, we were sitting there, and there was a book called Forever Amber. It was a sex story of the '40s. And that book, we had I think two copies in our group, and I had the book at the time, I was reading it. And when I finished someone was waiting for it, you know, it's like you get on the list now in the libraries, you're on the waiting list. And I was reading that book, and we were sitting there, and I was talking to this guy. And you could hear the guns. Well, then it got pretty intense, so they went into full -- so we went to our position, and we watched this guy come in. This Navy gunner where I was, boy, he was banging that plane, hitting it. He couldn't knock it down, it just kept on coming. And he hit the side of our LST, and torpedo went in the tank deck, and he hit topside. And we had a truck there with thousand pound bombs, about eight or 10 of them in this truck. As a matter of fact, some of the guys were sleeping in there, you know, at night, because it had a canvas top on it. And we slept on the deck most of the time the weather was decent. And boy, he hit that sucker and wiped that out. The plane did. Just -- the Navy fellows, they lost quite a few guys, you know. And then they couldn't get the pumps started. The day before, they were -- they had test runs with the pumps, they worked fine, but this torpedo must have damaged water lines and stuff like that. And mechanical, and they just couldn't get the pumps going. They tried. And the plane -- the boat was burning pretty good. And stuff was blowing up, you know, bombing, destroyer come over and tried to help us. And he had to back out because it got too hot, bombs going off. So we were told to abandon ship, boy, that's a long jump. You cross your legs and hope you don't straddle something and land in the water. That's how I got hurt. I got my face, burned my hands a little. And I got Purple Heart for that, they went into the burning gas.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You jumped into burning water?

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: Well, yeah, it was burning around the ship, that was -- it was all around the ship, you know, we had to get the heck out of there. We had -- there was one guy, he wasn't going to go overboard. And I remember this Navy guy, he just pulled out his pistol, he said well, I'll shoot you right here if you don't go. That guy was like a butterfly, boy, he went over. You didn't dive, you had to, you know, you were taught, you know, you knew how to -- you just didn't -- you jumped and you crossed your legs, and hung onto the -- I had the kapok, the old one, and you hold the top so it don't catch you under the chin. And into the water we went, you know, and then you hold up -- some of them kapoks, they weren't -- boy, they were like tying a stone around your neck. And some of the guys had the belts with the CO2, and they'd pop them. But I had this buddy, this Coffin couldn't swim, and I remember someone stole his life jacket. Boy, he was an upset puppy. He was -- he was going to shoot the SOB that stole his life jacket. But he went down the anchor chain. And a guy from Garfield Heights picked us up. He was in a PT boat, fished us out of the water, wanted to know what the heck we were doing there. This Coffin and him went to school together. And you know, I knew who he was, you know. But it was funny, you know, strange things happen, you know, that here this guy, you should meet like that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: The buddy that couldn't swim, he got out, he got rescued?

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: Oh, yeah, he grabbed a crate or --

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: Yeah, he had a crate or something he was floating on, but we were -- heck, we were half a mile or a mile offshore. It was a big bay. And they went into this place. That was the first train I saw over there, a sugar cane train, all little tracks, and that was a big thing on that island, they made -- Mindoro was sugar cane.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How long were you in the water before you were rescued?

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: Oh, about a half hour. You don't realize, I know they took us ashore, and we went into this LST, and all I had on was a pair of shorts, I don't know where the rest of the stuff -- I lost my watch, my ring. I had a nice pistol. And I got -- a guy got for me. And it was a nice thing. We weren't issued pistols, you know, we had carbines and machine guns and crap like that. But I had this nice pistol, and I took care of it. And I lost that. I got to shore, all I had -- I didn't even have the holster we had on it. But I remember stealing a pair of shoes on this LST, there was a mess of shoes there. I got myself a pair of shoes. Then they gave us clothes, they gave us shirt and some dungarees that the Navy had. And because we lost everything on the boat, you know. Our Navy finally sunk it. They have -- LST has compartments and they dog them down when they go into general quarters and they're air tight, and they're pretty hard to sink. You have to puncture a whole bunch of them to actually make it sink, but the Navy actually come up because it was -- had become a hazard out where it was so they got rid of it, you know. All of our stuff went to the bottom. But we lost a pilot in that water, he was coming back, and he crashed and -- in the ocean or into the bay, and that bay was full of barracuda, and they got him before they could get to him. They have -- at the end of the strips, they always have a crash boat, you know, if a pilot gets in trouble that they can, you know. And this guy, he was coming back, and he come in, and somehow he just -- whether the engines malfunctioned, but he went in. And before he could set out, before they could get to him, why they said there was -- you could see the water was all -- they were telling, you know, the barracuda or the fish must have got him. But that -- when we were there, there was so much shelling and stuff, I guess they took off. You know, they were smart ones, get out of the area, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: The barracuda were in the same water where you jumped?

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: Yeah, but --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: They had been scared away at that point?

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: Yeah, I would say, yeah, they were dropping bombs and stuff around through there and the Navy, big ships, a lot of noise. I imagine they -- that scares them, you know. They got -- but this was about a month later that this --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Pilot?

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: -- pilot went in there, unfortunately, they couldn't get to him fast enough, probably got trapped, he couldn't get the canopy open or something, maybe when they -- on his mission, maybe he got hit. He couldn't slide his canopy or pop his canopy open or something, you never know. But the plane, he was able to skid it in. While we were at Mindoro, too, there, when we were working on our P-38s and we were like oh, we were about three, four miles, maybe from the bay. The red alert went off, and they fire three guns in the air, everyone hunts a hole, you know. We were standing on the wing of our airplane, and we were working on it, and we were watching the bay and seen this one plane come down, and he dove, and there was a Liberty ship there. He dove right down, and it was a munition ship, and we're three, four miles from that bay. And we're on the wing, you know, and that plane was bouncing, actually darn near threw us off the wings, you know, they were bouncing. Well, we come down, and here comes some Jap planes down there, so boy, we peeled out of there, we run. And it was a big truck. I'll never forget that. There was a big truck there. Well, we dive underneath this big truck, you know, and this plane went da-da-da-da, you know, and you could hear them, you could see the stuff kicking up. And he disappeared. And they made a couple passes, we crawled out from underneath that sucker, and it was an -- it was a gasoline truck with the aviation gas. And any port in a storm, you know. You couldn't get below ground, you know. But we were in a revetment area, normally, you know, we shouldn't have been up where we were possibly, but you know, you're trying to get your plane back in service, and hey, they weren't bothering us, they were out in the bay. But where do you -- a couple of clowns come from, boy, they come scooting down there, they were da-da-da, and everyone -- and then our planes got involved in a real Christmas Eve, everyone was looking for the Jap Navy wondering where they were. Well, they were right off our island, and they shelled us. Boy, I'll tell you, you listen to them big -- them big 15-inch shells or whatever they had. They sound like freight trains going by. And they were after the strip. Well, anyhow, our planes, we -- they were looking for Halsey. Halsey was up north, and the Japs had snuck around. That was the story that I read in the books, you know, the history book when you get back. But I can relate to that, boy, I'll tell you, that was scary. But our old man, he put us -- bomb right down the stack of a Jap destroyer, and he blew that thing up, but it was beautiful. Our tracers, the Jap tracers coming up were green. And ours going down were orange. And they look like 4th of July, you know, but our planes would come in, and to land, to refuel and get gas and bombs and stuff, they had to turn their landing lights on. Well, they'd come in, flip them lights on, and we had vehicles positioned to put lights so, you know, you stay in between these things. Well, they were doing this, here come a Jap plane would follow him in and da-da-da-da, you know. We didn't lose any planes, but they sure as got your attention. And you're down there, and they're bombing this island and shelling, and you're working on your plane, getting them gas, and getting them loaded up and get them the hell out, you know. And the pilot was nervous, he didn't want to be there. He wanted to be back up where it was safe, you know. And they'd load them planes up, and away they'd go, you know, and then you'd hide somewhere. But everyone was busy, but I can remember that, boy, that that was -- that was something. And that -- when we're at Leyte, we were there at Leyte, that these pineapple -- they call them pineapple soldiers, they were in Hawaii. You know, first combat, and they're running around conditions red, conditions red. What the hell is condition red. Oh, the Japs are in the area. Jap airplane. Oh, you mean red alert. Boy, guy would get his gun, and bang, everyone would scatter, you know, but these clowns running around, condition red. That's what they were taught, you know. And the other guys, three shots and boy, hunt a hole, that's the way it worked, you know, or the antiaircraft would fire three. But it was something, and then the Japs, they used to send over these bombers, and their engines were out of sync, just they sent them over at night, and fly them, just -- you couldn't sleep. Eventually, you got so the hell with you, you just laid in bed and laid in your cot. And if you heard something whistle, roll over and fall on the ground, you know, hope like, you know, but they never -- we were always on the end of the strip or alongside of it. Because you know, close to the strip, and you're -- that's where they set our camp up. One way or another, you know, you were going to get it. If you were working, you had to be careful, back at your camp, you know. And they had moved a battery of 105, big antiaircraft, they were radar controlled. And they had them, and I never knew they were there, and I don't think anyone else in our camp knew they were there. And all of a sudden, this spotlight come on, and here's this looks like a moth up here, where's that Jap bomber. Radar -- boy, these four guns go off. I'll tell you, boy, I tell you that got your attention real quick. And then you could see the burst up around that airplane. And they finally, they drove him off. And one time, they actually -- it was something, boy, everyone was cheering and hollering, they hit him and down he come, you could see him, he was on fire. And away he went. He disappeared. But them guns, I'll tell you, they -- scared. I remember you laid there, and -- we were in the slit trench when them guns went off, boy, I'll tell you, I kicked some guy right in the face, you know, straightened out. We had a dog, a little Fox Terrier. This one guy was in Australia, and this Aussie soldier or sailor, soldier, asked him to watch the dog, he had to go to the John, little puppy. They had him in his -- the guy stole the dog, brought him back with us, and we had that dog all the way from New Guinea. And it never went on the boat. It always kept him back, and he flew. He'd come up with the air echelon. That dog would be laying in a tent or on someone's cot, you know. And all of a sudden he'd stand up and growl, and the hair, and he'd run, jump in a slit trench. It wasn't a few seconds later, the guns would go off and you couldn't throw that dog out of that slit trench, he'd take your arm off. Once the alert, he'd come out, he'd be just the nicest little puppy you ever wanted. Go back, whatever he was doing. But when that alert was on, don't mess with me. He was -- and they took him, the guy took him back, I guess he smuggled him, but they were up in I think it was -- I think it was Fort Lawton, up by Seattle, and he got run over by a truck. You know, he wasn't used to I guess -- a little more confused, down there where we were he could go anywhere he wanted, you know, and everyone knew him. And there wasn't a -- but those different incidents like that, you know, you have with that little dog, I mean, you know, everywhere we went, he went, you know. But then he gets back in the States and gets run over, you know. But that was something. Then we -- From Morotai, we went up, our planes worked over Luzon. Then they made the big invasion in Luzon, and as a matter of fact, I got a ride in one of our planes strafing up over Clark Field in Luzon. We come back, boy, I'll tell you, there was -- there were pieces of leaves where the metal joined on the undercarriage on the wings, they were going down, he was dropping napalm, and he had some small bombs, and strafing. And this guy, it was quite a ride. But I got --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you hit some --

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: Oh, yeah, they come right down across the top of them trees, you know, and he dropped his load, his napalm. And we come back, but it was -- that was the first time, the only time, but I did get a ride over Luzon, and it was interesting. But from then they were making their sweeps. And the Marines, they were doing their job, they caught different things. And then different islands. And that's where I saw my first B-29. Boy, that was a big airplane. I thought the 17 was big, but that looked like a peashooter alongside. As a matter of fact, they could put our P-38 under the wing, you know. And we got to see -- I got to see one of them, looked at it real close. And it was a big, big airplane. And then from there, we went to Okinawa. And we landed at Ie Shima.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How soon after the invasion did you land on Ie Shima?

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: We -- I forget what the infantry was, as a matter of fact, the fellow out here was in the invasion of Ie Shima, and we were sitting like I say, that's when the Kamikazes really, really raised heck up there off Okinawa. We sat on it, we were on an LST, and they had taken the island, and we got there a day or so after they had, you know, taken it. And there was a huge air strip there. The Japanese -- well, they had it there I think to protect the homeland. And they had a hill called -- they called it Million Dollar Hill, the Navy must have shelled that for a week. And even this guy was telling me, even while we were making the invasion, they were bombing or blowing this hill because the Japs had it honeycombed with caves. And he said we got up there, boy, he says it was terrible. That's when Ernie Pyle got killed. He was with this thing, they were coming along the road and a sniper got him. And then they took that group once the island was secure, Ie Shima, the Marines were making the initial landing on Okinawa, and while these guys were taken to Okinawa, and --

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: No, we stayed on Ie Shima. And I went to Okinawa a couple times, we had an airplane land over there, and they sent us over to -- get it, recover it, you know, and if we needed parts or if it wasn't flyable, you know, strip it, what we could and bring it back. I did get to see that Shuri Castle, it was -- that was where the Japs had walls 20-foot thick, it was a huge castle.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Where was this, I didn't --

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: In Okinawa, Shuri Castle, yeah. This friend of mine out here, he was a machine gunner in the infantry. He says they took that castle. And he says finally, boy, he says that was something. And then our planes escorted the Jap peace envoy down, these Betty bombers were painted snow white and had big green crosses on the side. And our planes flew up to Japan and escorted them down. And they landed on Ie Shima, and they had this big C-54, which is a -- became a main passenger plane, that type of -- after the war when the flying became so prominent, why, that type of plane was used. It was a huge bugger. And these Japs come on, you know. I have pictures of it. This old colonel giving the guy -- I'll get your butt on the damn plane, don't -- no. And then --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: The Japanese tried to shake his hand?

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: No. Yeah. But anyhow, what was really funny, that night we escorted the planes, them Betty bombers were sitting on the strip down -- the Japs come over, they bombed the hell out of that island. They were a real pain in the butt, they were dropping bombs, just real nasty. But the planes had gone down to the Philippines where MacArthur was, and I guess where his staff and whatever, Halsey, and the Navy -- well, what was his name, I can't remember his name, he was --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Nimitz?

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: Nimitz and MacArthur, then they come up with the agreement.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So this air raid on Ie Shima on the air field is after the second atomic bomb was dropped?

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Before they dropped the bomb?

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: It was after the bomb --

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: Yeah --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: + signed the papers?

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: It was before they signed the paper, the bombs had already been dropped, and they had come down to, you know, to make up their -- what they wanted and were willing to, you know, that was a big --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How many air raids did you encounter between that time before the papers --

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: Just that one night, they bombed the hell out of the place, then they put up a lot of air cover. And well, what it was, a lot of Kamikazes coming around, you know, and the Navy, they took a beating, the Navy, the picket lines they had, you read the back -- I don't know if you ever read it, but it's a book called Okinawa, Stephen --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Ambrose?

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: Ambrose wrote it. And this -- as a matter of fact, this fellow's a friend of mine, I almost fell out of the chair, Earl Miller, Troy, Ohio. Whoa.

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: But he had sent him a letter and asked him, you know, and that was quite interesting. But those picket lines, they must have been something. That -- poor Navy guys, they, you know --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you hear about any Kamikaze attacks after the -- in that time period --

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: No, no, that ended.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That one nasty air raid?

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: Oh, yeah, we just -- it was just --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was it the same day they had flown in?

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: They had flown in, got up a C-54, went up to the Philippines --

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: Yeah, they were gone.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -- air raid that night?

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: That night, they bombed the hell out of us, you know. But that's the way, that's the way they were. Peace, they hadn't declared peace. You were still open.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: War was still on as far as they were concerned?

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: Yeah, and then finally, we went over to -- we did go to Okinawa. We were at Okinawa, we got set up, you know, everyone was, how many points you got, oh, boy. You got -- I had a Purple Heart, I get an extra five points. Guys had Silver Stars, some guys had this, oh, boy, I got extra points. Well, they start, you know, getting everyone home. And they took us to Okinawa, that's where you -- was a staging area. We were over there, boy, they had a storm. I never seen such -- you didn't go out, you had to wear your pot, the steel helmet. And one guy had been -- they had these corrugated roofs, you know, the metal, one guy got -- a couple guys got hurt, one guy actually got decapitated. That thing was just -- the wind. And he was going to chow, and that wind just come, hit him, and just cut the top of his head, it was just like a knife.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Blew the helmet, the strap --

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: Yeah, didn't have his helmet on.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, he didn't have his helmet on?

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: No, just had a -- we had like a baseball cap, fatigue hat, we just -- I never wore a helmet. Only time I wore a helmet is like when we'd move or take a bath.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So the wind decapitated him?

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: Yeah, the wind hit this piece of metal, and it just --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, it just --

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: Yeah, a lot of people, the wind, I guess they -- it was a typhoon or something. And then about oh, a couple days later it was all over. But boy, the orders come down, everyone will go -- you wear your steel helmet, you know, you don't go -- and you be careful where you're going because, you know, the storm. But this guy was going to mess hall. And we were in a staging area, and then we got on the boat, and the guy that brought us home, the captain of the boat wanted to be home for Thanksgiving. And boy, he pounded that ship. And we did, we landed Thanksgiving eve in Seattle. And in the barracks, we had a fellow named Joe Sweats that went home ahead of me, ahead of us. He met every boat that come in, he'd go to the barracks, hey, any 35th fighter in here. We had -- he always had a bottle. He was telling us, we were there about three or four days, getting new clothes. All I ever wore, cut off khakis, and the shirts, the sleeves, you cut them out, it was always hot, you know. And it was cold in Okinawa. I wore a jacket in Okinawa. I had our regular -- I wish I had one of them now, them are pretty good jackets. But that was -- then we come home, and then I went to Camp Adaberry and got discharged.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So it was your squadron that -- backtracking a second, your squadron escorted the Japanese envoys up to the Philippines?

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: No, no, just down.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Escorted the Betty bombers down +

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: From Japan, yeah, to Ie Shima, and they landed the plane, and then our planes landed, and then the C-54, I don't know who escorted that, but I would imagine someone escorted it. There wasn't our planes, and they went on down to the Philippines, to Luzon, where Nimitz and all the big-wigs were. And I guess some of the politicians were there, everyone wanted to get in on the act, you know. And --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: +. Go ahead.

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: Then they had signed and they agreed, and you know the results, what, they met on the Missouri and everything. And we went home.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I think the question is obvious because you were reading a book, was that Kamikaze attack in -- that you were -- where you were hurt was a daylight attack; right?

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did they usually attack during the day?

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: They attacked any time they want, you know, they just -- they're in the area. They could see better during the day, you know, they were only given I guess so much gas. And they were a flying bomb. That's -- it was divine wind, that was their -- you know, but we had them during the day where they'd come in. And I don't know if they hit a big field, there was nothing there, I don't know what he was thinking of, maybe he didn't want to go back. He just went right in the field, blew a big whole. And I don't know if they ever caught a couple, I think they caught a couple. I can't be sure about that, the rumor, you know, but some -- I don't think all of them wanted to die. But the bigger part of them did. But you know, look at how after the war, the guy was what, two years living off the land.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Even longer?

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: Yeah, yeah. And he come down, they caught him. We had a guy -- we had a guy come in, I forget where in the heck it was, Biak, stole food right out of the mess hall. See, being in the Air Force was a lot easier, when we went into it, we set our camp up, they build a mess hall. It was screened in, you know, you didn't have to eat your food out in -- with all the flies all over it and that. And they had your cleaning pits for your big tubs with boiling water and that. And when you ate, you dunk your mess kit in that thing, you know, and that sterilized and they put things. And then you always had a medic sitting there making you take your Atabrine. Oh, that was bitter, you know. You take the Atabrine and then --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's the stuff that would turn you yellow?

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: Yeah, everyone was afraid they were going to be sterile. They didn't like, you know, I don't want -- but they'd sit right there and boy, and they had these bottles of pills right on the table, and you better take them, you know. And then they had a medic, it depended upon the area, too, but I always took them, they didn't bother me, you know. But a lot of guys, they didn't want to take them. But they were funny, you'd leave one in your pocket and you wash your clothes, they were yellow. It was really something to watch, you know. But the mess, the garbage, you'd see they were all -- yellow, guys that throw them in there, they'd spit them out.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You were saying the Japanese soldier came down and was stealing from the mess hall?

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: Yeah, come down, they had a tent there off from the mess hall, and they kept their supplies there. Somehow he got down there and stole some stuff out. They were accusing the guys because, you know, we used to make jungle juice and that. And boy, the cooks would get a jug or two out of it. But we had a big acid bottle, and this acid bottle, they cleaned it up, you put water in, and they'd make like a sheep pie or a cake where you take the squeezings, and you put it in this and you put some yeast and sugar, and you put a poncho around it, and a light bulb, and that thing would cook. And this jungle juice, the maggots used to come up on the top, and you'd scrape them suckers off, you know. And boy, you watch it, and you'd put your hand in that jar, it would be hot. Because it's fermenting, you know, and pretty soon, you know, it's drinkable. And it depended what type of fruit they gave you, but most of the time it was -- I can remember looked like raspberry. And you'd scrape that off, you know, and strain it. And then you'd give the cook a cup, he gave you the stuff, you know, and --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Powerful stuff?

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: Oh, yeah, knock you right on your butt, jungle juice, everyone had a -- you know, maybe three, four tents would get together, you know, and when you moved, when you moved, boy, that jar was -- that jug was protected. Same way they had a still down to the motor pool, I remember they had a still, when we moved, that was the first thing that was loaded on the truck. They take that sucker down, had the coils in, pack that real good, because they made their own moonshine some of them guys did. My mother used to send me hops. She sent me hops. The only trouble is -- and she sent me beer caps. But you couldn't get beer bottles and beer bottles with a cap has a certain lip on it. Well, one of the guys down at the maintenance shop, he made a press that we could cap the bottles, but they were whiskey bottles. Well, you'd put them around your -- each tent where you had your little table that you made around the tent pole, and a bench, and you would sit and write your letters and, you know, and middle of the night, something, pow, pow, they'd blow off because -- everyone would get up, you get up in the morning. (Laughing.) That was another thing, it got real tough, boy, some of these guys get drinking that damn jungle juice and stuff, and they go down and get on the plane, they take a big whiff of oxygen off the airplane, you know, take a -- clear your head right up real quick. And then they would get beer, and damn guy take a fire extinguisher, you had cold beer right, squirt it over. That CO2, it got so bad, jeez, they'd go to use the fire extinguisher, use the fire extinguisher, the damn things would be empty because some clown cooled his beer, you know. But we didn't get -- we got beer issues every now and then, which they gave us and stuff like that. And it was Golden Grain. Oh, it was a terrible tasting beer. Come from Kansas. I remember -- I remember South Dakota, Golden Grain, you go to the PX, and boy, that was terrible stuff. You drink that, but hey, most of it was 3.2, I don't think it was that 6 percent beer.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: The officers just turn, look the other way at this jungle juice?

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: Oh, they got some of it, too, you know. But it was good. You'd have a little -- have a little snooker of it, you know, go -- you'd go to eat, you'd have a little snooker, but it didn't last long. You make your big jug and pass it around to everyone, you know, each tent got some samplings, you know, but everyone contributed to it. But we had a club, everyone -- payday threw a buck into this pot. The officers did the same thing. Well, they'd fly down to Australia, they'd buy booze. Okay. The officers had theirs, we had ours. And we made two big tanks, hung them on the plane. When they'd move, the air echelon, this one -- tanks were hung on this one plane, and he was in the middle of the pack. And he protected -- that was his job to get that, and the dummy, this one guy dropped them. Boy, they were ready to kill that guy. Dropped both tanks. They got jumped, so he -- you know, they dropped their tanks. And instead of him, you know, hanging back, he was going to get -- and he dropped the tank, boy, I tell you, people didn't want to talk to that guy. But then everyone started up their collection again, you know. But that's what they do, they'd go down, they'd go down for parts or something, and you know, your officer, you'd give him -- he'd get his money, you know, then he'd go down, and they were good that way. Everybody, you know, looked out for everyone. But I can remember that tank, boy, they were really upset. He dropped the damn booze into the ocean, you know. But they weren't -- the guys weren't drunks or that, you know, hey, you have a little snooker every now and then, what the hell, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you do much souvenir collecting or any of the guys in your squadrons?

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: We never -- we never got that close to really get -- the infantry used to come in, and they'd have flags and they'd have stuff like that. And you know, you had a bottle of booze or you had stuff, you know, where you'd trade them, you know. And we had a guy used to make these ammunition chutes on an airplane were all stainless steel, and boy, they were priceless. They'd -- that plane would be sliding down the runway all wrecked up, they'd get the chute because they used to make wrist bands for your watch. And the leather bands, about a week or two weeks, they'd rot, you know. And people didn't have metal so they'd make these things, they just -- you slide them on and your watch was sitting on the top, and they had two things to hold the watch, you know, and your pin. And they used to make them. Well, the infantry guys would come in, you know, and they'd swap stuff like that, they'd take stuff like that or booze, cigarettes, you know, you had cigarettes. Your C rations and that, gave you a -- little packs, maybe, four packs, used to give them away up in the streets years ago, advertise cigarettes, four cigarettes to this little -- well, you used to get things like that. And they were free. They were in your meals. And then they had a chocolate. They had chocolate. You need a sledge hammer, it didn't melt, you know. You gnawed on it, you couldn't, you know, break it off in pieces, but it was made that it wouldn't melt, you know, in the hot temperature. And them things were always barter, you know. Something like that. But it was different. Like this one guy in our tent, his brother was a paratrooper, he dropped in Carigador (ph), they had an outfit that protected the strip, that was this outfit's job. And he'd come over and him and his buddies would come over once in a while, they'd have souvenirs, you know. Flags. But a lot of these guys, they made their own flags, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: + a parachute?

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I heard about that.

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: Paint the circle red, hey, I got an original Jap --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: U.S. Army or something in the corner?

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: Yeah, I had a Jap flag, I got a -- I got mine in New Guinea, I got it up in Finch Haven. I lost it, went down with the boat when we lost -- it was a nice flag. It was -- someone was -- I guess he was carrying it on his body. I don't know how I did get it. But I did have an original, it was silk, and it was a nice -- another thing they used to look for is the headbands the Japs used to wear. They -- Kamikaze pilots wore them. But our pilots had the regular helmet, they didn't wear like a bandana. Some of them I guess, the planes were hot when they were sitting on the ground, they'd wear something like that to keep the -- you know, but the Japs, they had pictures, books that I read, they had a white band they used to wear. It was a letter of good will or something that their thousand stitches, everyone had a sign of -- I've seen a few of those that some of the guys had that they --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you tell me there was a prayer on the headband or something?

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: Yeah, they had a prayer. It was the family would make this, it was like a good luck thing, the family would make it. If I remember it was like a thousand stitches. The mother would have everyone, you know, put a stitch in, and then they would send it. It was different colored, some of them were black, but it was on like a white headband, and they flew it as for good luck, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Very good.

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: But then I come home, and I went back to work and went back to the Erie Railroad and met my wife, she worked in the thing, and we had two children, and --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When you think about your experiences overseas, does any particularly vivid memory come to mind?

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: The thing like getting bombed in strafe, but otherwise, no, it was -- it was -- it was something I think I value because it changed my life. It made me -- it made me grow up, let's put it that way. And I felt like I did a job, I did my job. And it was enjoyable. I saw things that I'd never see. I wished I had the money to go back to all the places I've been back, you know, boy, that would be something. But really, to go overseas and do that, and the comradeship, you know. I had some good friends, you know. I lost a few good friends. But this buddy of mine, this Coffin and I, him and I, we got along real good, you know. He was from Cleveland. There was eight of us from Cleveland. And when you come back, why, you lose, lose track. I moved a lot. We moved. I think we moved five times. We were like a yo-yo. We lived in Hornell, New York. We lived in Scranton. Come back to Cleveland. Went back to New York. Back to Cleveland. We ended up in New York City, and I retired. You know, so you lose contact with your friends. No, it was an adventure. I think most of the guys -- some guys had it worse than others. You know, I'm just thankful that I come back. I didn't get hurt. You know, there's a lot of guys that come back that, you know, they were mentally hurt. But I was a kid, you know. When you're a kid, you don't think of them serious things, you know. Someone's going to shoot you, you know. And I imagine they felt the same way, you know. But we were called to do a job. And that's what we did. I -- when I went overseas, you know, when I went overseas with my Army overcoat, wool, wool pants, wool shirt, and it was 100 degrees, 90, 100 degrees, I was sweating my brains out, but figured it out after a while, you know. I brought the stuff over because some guy was going back home, probably ended up, took it back. But I hope he wasn't a big guy because I had short legs, you know, he was going to be in some big trouble.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So that's what you did, you would turn in your uniforms?

sp.speaker: Edwin Leferink
sp.p: Yeah, we got over there, they gave us khakis, you know, the khakis, they give them were new, you know, you got new khakis. But there was guys going back, they were going back to cold weather and the climate so they had to have something, you know. END OF CD.
